source_text: Verum cum nihil horum quae diximus baptizatorum constet evenire corporibus, non potuisse autem aliter, id est non debuisse, quam his medicinae modis totum fieri veritas clarior sole monstraverit, confitendum tibi est aut illa, quae prius enumeravimus, non accidisse peccato et ideo nec vulnera fuisse naturae, ut constet ratio gratiae, per quam manifestum est illa de suis ordinibus mota non esse, aut certe negandum in mysteriis Christi quidquam esse medicinae, quae de tot secundum te morbis ne unum quidem sanare potuerunt.
pass_a_gloss: But since none of these things which we have said is established to happen to the bodies of the baptized, but that it could not otherwise, that is ought not, than by these modes of medicine the whole be done, truth clearer than the sun has shown, it must be confessed by you either that those things which we enumerated earlier did not happen to sin and therefore were not wounds of nature, so that the account of grace may stand, through which it is manifest that those things have not been moved from their orders, or certainly it must be denied that in the mysteries of Christ there is anything of medicine, which from so many diseases according to you have not been able to heal even one.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS vulnus; Blaise sin as wound

pass_b_english: But none of these things we have mentioned is known to happen to baptized people’s bodies. And truth, clearer than the sun, has shown that full healing could not—or rather should not—take place except by these methods of treatment. You must therefore confess either that the things we listed earlier did not arise through sin and so were not wounds of nature, thus preserving a coherent account of grace, which plainly has not displaced them from their order; or else you must deny that Christ’s mysteries contain any medicine at all, since they have not been able to heal even one of the many diseases you describe.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
